title: Comforted to comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3–4)
hookLine: the God of all comfort comforts us so we can comfort others

lines: TWO WOMEN AT A KITCHEN TABLE.
SHE LEARNED IT AT HER OWN TABLE.
cards: Two women at a kitchen table. One lost her husband last month, and the house is full of flowers she doesn't know what to do with. The other lost hers years ago.
She doesn't make a speech. She knows which casseroles freeze well. She knows the second month can be harder than the first, when the cards stop coming.
She knows not to say he's in a better place unless she's asked. She learned it at her own kitchen table, from someone who sat with her. Paul has a line for exactly this.

teach.b: It's how Paul opens his second letter to Corinth, the letter of the past few days.

In the King James words: "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

teach.h: FIVE COMFORT WORDS IN TWO VERSES.
teach.b: Count the comfort words: comfort, comforteth, comfort, comfort, comforted. Five, in two verses. It starts with God, the God of all comfort.
It reaches us in all our tribulation. And it doesn't stop there: that we may be able to comfort others.
Comfort, in this letter, isn't a pool you sit in. It's a river. It comes in so it can go out.
Paul isn't writing from a calm desk, either.

A few verses later he says that in Asia they were "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." So this comfort isn't advice from someone who's never been under it. It's been tested.
That's why the widow at the kitchen table helps. Not because she suffered, as if suffering were the qualification, but because she was comforted, and remembers how it was done.
Some readers see in this a picture of how a church works: the comforted becoming comforters, so no one's comfort ends with them.

how: Christians comfort one another through visits, meals, prayer and simply sitting with people who grieve, and some churches run grief groups or care teams in which people who have been through a loss support others going through the same.

o: learning to cheer yourself up without anyone's help
a reward God gives only after suffering has ended
receiving God's comfort so it can reach others in trouble

games.q: comforted to comfort — tap the pairs.
p: to comfort them which are in any trouble

s: Paul writes about comfort as someone who had never despaired
he tells the Corinthians that in Asia "we despaired even of life."
in 2 Corinthians 1, God's comfort is meant to stop with the one who receives it
it comes "that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble."
Paul calls God the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort
both names are in his opening blessing, 2 Corinthians 1:3.

games.q: you're Paul. you've come through trouble so heavy you despaired even of life, and God comforted you. what do you write that the comfort was for?
o: proof that you were right all along.
so you can comfort others in any trouble.
a private gift, to keep to yourself.
games.why: "that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." the comfort is meant to move.

practice: Remember a time someone comforted you, who it was and what they actually did, maybe food, or silence, or a text on the hard date without being asked.
Then think of someone going through something like what you went through, and picture that same comfort passed on to them; if you pray, you can name them before God.
And if you're in a stretch where even life feels too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Comforted to comfort. Paul's picture of God's comfort as a river: it reaches us in our trouble so it can reach others in theirs.

orig.note: Greek: comfort, encouragement; the God of all comfort, 2 Corinthians 1:3.

carryVoice: Your line: pass the comfort on. It starts, Paul writes, with the God of all comfort. See you tomorrow.
